 Walter Koenig, forever iconic to the sci-fi world as Pavel Chekov on the original Star Trek , has passed away at the age of 90. Per a statement from Galactic Productions , the actor and writer passed away at his North Hollywood home, “surrounded by his daughter and niece.”
 Koenig was born in Chicago in 1936; the child of Russian Jewish immigrants, he did not pursue acting until after college. He made his screen debut in 1963, appearing in the first two episodes of General Hospital , but did not continue on with the long-running soap opera. Instead, he became a key cast member on Gene Roddenberry’s groundbreaking sci-fi adventure series, leaning hard into his character’s Russian accent when he was brought on board for Season 2. The presence of a Russian officer on the bridge of the U.S.S. Enterprise was a significant move for the 1960s science fiction show , considering that most Americans (and American pop culture) considered Russians to be the enemy during the height of the Cold War.
 Star Trek dominated the rest of Koenig’s career, as he continued playing Chekov in the six Star Trek feature films that followed the show’s cancellation. (Chekov did not appear in the 1970s animated series, but Koenig did write the episode “The Infinite Vulcan” for the show.) He also made a voice cameo for the final episode of Star Trek: Picard as “President Anton Chekov,” implied to be the son of Pavel — with the character’s first name serving as an homage to the late actor Anton Yelchin, who played Chekov in J.J. Abrams’ three Star Trek films.

 Beyond Star Trek , Koenig made a striking impression on the series Babylon 5 , on which he played a powerful telepath and duplicitous adversary for the space station crew. His other TV credits include Columbo , Ironside , Bring ‘Em Back Alive , and voice work on The Real Ghostbusters ; he also made a cameo as himself on Futurama in 2002, alongside other surviving members of the original Star Trek cast.
 Fellow cast member George Takei remembered him in an Instagram post Monday morning, sharing that:
 “Walter and I met on the bridge of the Enterprise in the 1960s, and we stayed friends for nearly six decades. When Brad and I married in 2008, Walter stood beside us as our best man. Just last month, on Sept. 14, he turned 90, on the same day Brad and I celebrated our 18th wedding anniversary. I will always treasure that he and I shared that date.
 “Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too.
 “Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.”
